PLANS FOR THE CONVENTION
ANNOUNCEMENT
has been made of
1 the plans for the 106th Convention of
Psi Upsilon, to be held in the 115th Year
of the Fraternity, with the Tau Chapter act
ing as host.
The Convention wiU be held in Phila
delphia, on the 16th, 17th and 18th of
June. Due to the fact that two national
poHtical conventions are to be held in Phila
delphia in June and July, it was impossible
to secure hotel accommodations. Arrange
ments have, however, been made with the
University of Pennsylvania, so that all dele
gates can be housed in a
University doiinitory a block away from the Chapter House.
Delegates and other guests arriving on
the 16th should get off at the 30th Street
Station, Philadelphia, and go direct to the
Chapter House. If they arrive on
Thursday
morning, June 17, from New York, they
should get off at the North Philadelphia
Station and take a taxi dhect to the Phil
adelphia Cricket Club.
Registration is to be at the Chapter
House. Rooms are to be provided in a Uni
versity dormitory at 36th Street and Spruce,
just a block from the Chapter House.
The Convention will open with a Smoker
on Wednesday evening, June 16th. On
Thursday mornuig, followuig breakfast at
the Chapter House, buses will take all dele
gates to the Philadelphia Cricket Club for
business sessions. Following the morning
session, luncheon will be served around
noon. After the afternoon session, there will
be opportunities for golf, swimming and
tennis. There will be an informal dinner,
and members will be transported back to
the Chapter House by bus.
On Friday, the Convention will follow
the same
pattern as on
Thursday, except
that the day will end with the Convention
banquet in the evening. This will be In
formal. Albert C. Jacobs, Phi '21, Provost
of Columbia University, recently elected
member of the Executive Council, will be
toastmaster at the banquet.

HISTORY of the Tau Chapter
has been prepared by William P.
Harbeson, '06, as Editor, ably assisted by
John D. E. Spaeth, '88, Henry N. Woolman,
'96, and George T. Sharpe, '11. In the
Annals of Psi Upsilon is a shorter account
of the Tau, and it would be well if the
delegates would read this before attending
the Convention in June.
The Tau was the brain-child of Dr.
Charles S. Dolley, Pi '78, who in 1884 was
on the faculty of the University of Pennsyl
vania. Dr. Dolley naturally wanted to see
his Fraternity represented in Pennsylvania,
by a
group of men devoted to scholarship,
men from outside Philadelphia as well as
from the city; and above all living in a
fraternity house as their home. He talked
over these matters with some of his stu
dents, leaders in the classes of 1887 and
1888. An association was
gathered together
called Upsilon Kappa. The first entry in the
minutes of Upsilon Kappa is the statement
that the first object was to become a
chapter
of Psi Upsilon. Four years later. May 5,
1891, they were admitted.
The first quarters taken were a set of
rooms at 3613 Locust Street. Their first
home was No. 206 De Kalb Square. The
second house occupied a
strategic lot at 300
South Thirty-sixth Street, where it could
municate as
promptly as
possible with
Brother Donald F. Torrey, Tau '14, Chair
man, Architects' Building, Philadelphia 3,
Pennsylvania. Telephone: Rittenhouse 65146.
Other members of the Convention Com
mittee are:
Henry N. Woolman, Tau '96
(member of the Executive Council of Psi
Upsilon), H. Walter Rowan, Tau '43, Paul
Kitchen, Tau '48 (Head of the Tau Chap
ter), Walter Black, Tau '49, Charles M.
Boswell, Xi '18, Henry K. Kurtz, Eta '14,
Sidney Jenkins, Gamma '14, John F. Arndt,
Iota '21, Burton K. Hollister, Beta '08.
literally look down on the campus. "The
Castle," present home of the Tau, which
the chapter occupied in 1900, occupies the
same lot. Henry P. Erman, '04, headed a
campaign to pay off the floating debt in its
entirety. This was
finaUy accomplished due
in large part to Henry N. Woolman,

full.
Then the "City of Brotherly Love" raised
the assessment to a hundred and fifty thou
sand dollars. The chapter was forced to
deed the property over to the University to
be used as college dormitories, with a re
version clause which states that should the
university at any time cease to use the prop
erty as a
college dormitory, title will be re
turned to the Psi Upsilon of Philadelphia.
Thus, "The Castle" no
longer belongs to
the chapter except in the larger sense, for it
remains a monument, hallowed by years of
recollection.
The Tau had its first Convention in 1901
and its second in 1920. The Diamond is
sure that the delegates to the 1948 Conven
tion will return with the conviction that the
Tau and its alumni body, the Psi Upsilon of
Philadelphia, are an
important and vital

George Abbott, Upsilon
'
1 1
By Albert J. Elias, Upsilon '46
THERE
are three things m the present
day theater which continue to attract
the most attention: The Voice of Tallulah
Bankhead, The Legs of Gertrude Law
rence, and The Pace of a
George Abbott
show. Tallulah can mesmerize the audience
with her deep chest tones and Gertie can
dazzle them with her shapely limbs�but
it takes the Abbott Touch to mesmerize
and dazzle and whirl the customers about.
George Abbott, as
producer and direc
tor, has brought to plays and musicals alike
a
hght hand, the most suitable word to
describe the Abbott Touch being "lively."
Admittedly, the dizzy pace sometimes
sends a show tumbhng rather than spin
ning; the kick in the pants proves too much
and it falls flat on its face, badly bruised
and, usually, quickly withdrawn from cir
culation. More often than not, however,
Abbott manages to bring to the pleasant
but unimportant inaterial with which he
works a sense of real dramatic action; his
characters may be loud and brassy, but
they are ahve; and the speed with which
things move
may be breathtaking, but the
play breathes hfe, is never
stagnant or
dead. If it sometimes exhausts, at least
it never bores. And while it never shakes
the earth, it does keep moving.
At the moment the Broadway shovraian
is represented by two shows, "Look, Ma,
I'm Dancin'
"
and "High Button Shoes,"
both successful musicals. Yet it is a slow
season for a man who once, ten years ago,
had four shows running simultaneously in
New York.
Abbott has been prospering in the
theater for thirty-five years as author, ac
tor and director, sometimes all three at
once. At the University of Rochester,
where he was an
undergraduate, he first
stumbled onto the stage between numbers
of the Glee Club and, in a
badly fitting
suit, recited dramatic monologues. He be
longed to the dramatic club and not only
acted eccentric old men with wobbly legs
but also, as director, knocked a
play around
for the first time.
After being graduated in 1911, he went
on to George Pierce Baker's seminar at
Harvard and from then on was hell bent on
becoming a
playwright. Baker was
turning
out no second Eugene O'Neill in this stu
dent, but he did make Abbott a serviceable
enough playwright�one who, when he left
Baker's tutelage, resorted to acting only as
a
stopgap against the day when his first
play should be produced.
His professional debut was as a drunken
college boy in a
play called "The Mis
leading Lady," but his success there was
short-lived and soon he was playing Nu
bian slaves in vaudeville and working in
stock companies. Over a two year period
he earned all of $800.
Abbott was 29 when he finally found
himself in a hit, "Daddies," starring the
celebrated Jeanne Eagles, and in which he
played the father of triplets. It was, how
ever, during the tour of "Dulcy," a
comedy
by the budding team of Kaufrnan and Hart
which starred Lynn Fontanne, that his ca
reer took the greatest leap forward. For
one of his fellow players was
James Gleason and with him, during time spent traveUing and in sitting backstage on wardrobe
trunks waiting for their few and farbetween entrances, he vtrote "The Fall
Guy." The comedy was
produced two
years later, in 1925, and Abbott was
pro
grammed as an author for the first time
and as a director, too.
It was also in the tour of "Dulcy" that
Abbott met a
yoimg understudy, Ann Pres
ton
Bridgers, and from their ooUaboration
came "Coquette," the play about a tragic
Southern flirt which, when it was finally
produced five years later, sent Helen Hayes
on the road to stardom.
Abbott, then, had given up acting and
had estabhshed himself both as author
and dhector. Until as
recently as 1934, it
is true, he did act on occasion�in such

roles as
John Brown, the Second Yeoman
in a revival of "The Yeoman of the Guard,"
and he sang a
cowboy's lament in Maxwell
Anderson's first hit, "The White Desert."
But the need for acting was over, once he
had been recognized as an author.
He may have been recognized, but he
was
really not acclaimed until "Broadway,"
the melodrama which he wrote with
Phihp Dunning and which, because it was
a hit, served to induce him to produce
plays himself. "But when I turned pro
ducer after this show," he recalls, "the
only scripts people would submit to me
were
gangster plays, melodramas of one
sort or another. I was
typed. So I was
glad
to be able to come across with 'May Meets
Girl,' which, presented in 1935, was
my
first show in the dual capacity of director
and producer."
That was the beginning of what might
be knovwi as George Abbott's Early, or
Farcical Period. During this time he pro
duced, directed and often collaborated on
a
long list of such comedies as "Brother
Rat," "Room Service," "What a Life," and
"Kiss and Tell." These were farces where
the laughs could be clocked and the timing
was
impeccable. These were the plays
where the Abbott Touch succeeded emi
nently weU. Then, of course, there were
such minor calamities as "Snafu" and
Saroyan's "Get Away, Old Man," which
found Abbott propelling his characters
through this flimsy material and about the
stage�more as in cartwheels than as in
life.
His Farcical Period has been supplanted
�or, if not supplanted, at least supple
mented�by his Musical Period. He was di
recting an
elephant and Jimmy Durante
for Billy Rose's "Jumbo" when he became
interested in musical shows. Consequently,
two years later, he took a
Shakespeare play
off the shelf, dusted it off, eliminated a
line, then a verse, a scene, a character,
asked Rodgers to supply music, and
emerged with "The Boys from Syracuse,"
a variation of the Bard's "Comedy of
Errors." Since then he has been involved
with "Too Many Girls," "Pal Joey," "Rest
Foot Forward," "On the Town," "Billion
Dollar Baby," "Barefoot Boy With Cheek,"
and, now, "High Button Shoes" and "Look,
Ma."
Abbott denies having a
predilection for
any one
type show, although his career
speaks otherwise. He obviously prefers
comedies that deal with adolescence. And
just as he likes plays about youth, so, too,
does he like youthful players. He says he
enjoys directing young players, as
yet undefiled by movieland, and he finds them
more
pliable and susceptible to direction
than veterans. Abbott may not work with
name stars but, it is interesting to note,
he does develop them�Gene Kelly, Eddie
Albert, June Allyson, Eddie Bracken,
Gene Tierney, June Havoc, Van Johnson,
and Nancy Walker.
Having been on the stage himself, Ab
bott's direction of a
play stems from his
own
experience as an actor. Abbott re
hearsals are rehearsals; Abbott actors are
actors. He hoots at the "romanticists who
live and feel" their plays. He sets his
scenes
mentally before the first rehearsal
and on the very first day has the actors on
their feet and well into their parts. "There
are no table conferences," he points out.
"No 'What-do-you-think' stuff or
any
dawdling didoes." Abbott's way with a
script is first to have it read by a
group
of friends, among whom may be some ac
tors. WTiile they read he takes notes, but
says nothing. After that he calls in the
authors and they prepare the script for
production. He goes ahead when he "feels
ready."
He takes actors into his confidence and
won't hesitate to say, "This scene is wrong,
but let's leave it until we
try the show on
the road." With playwrights, however, Ab
bott is reputedly less gentle. One story has
it that an author who stayed up all night
to rewrite a scene and the next morning
showed it to Abbott, once said playfully,
"Well, the mountain labored and I hope
it brought forth a mouse." Abbott read the
scene without changing expression and re
marked, "No, no. The mountain labored
and brought forth a louse. Let's go to the
theater."
He is unlike most of his colleagues- when
it comes to his opinion of theater critics.
"Fortunately or unfortunately, as it may

78 THE DIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON
affect the individual producer," he says,
"the critics are 99 per cent of the time
right when they agree, and for this reason,
if for no other, they're a
great economic
asset to the theater . . .
they do the theater
a lot of good service. Mark you, I don't
say pleasant service, but utilitarian, which
any producer in his right mind ought to
acknowledge."
George Abbott hardly fits the popular
definition of a
Big Producer�a
tough-talk
ing exhibitionist who wears a lecherous
expression, Lucius Beebe clothes and a
diamond ring, smokes a
big cigar, drinks
champagne from pink ballet slippers, lives
in a
penthouse, and gives lavish parties.
Fifty-nine-year-old Abbott is tall, broadshouldered, his remaining blond hairs cut
short, his eyes blue, his expression happy.
He dresses in plain shirts and dark suits.
As someone once said, he looks like the
vice-president of a branch bank. He hardly
ever swears, never smokes, and drinks only
when absolutely necessary, disliking even
wine unless it "tastes like orangeade."
Once, at a dance on
Long Island, he aston
ished his companions by downing a
glass
of champagne. "I drank it," he now admits,
"so I wouldn't smell the liquor on
my part
ner's breath."
His most worldly passion is dancing and
playing croquet, or
any game in which he
can
participate. In Long Island, where he
spends his summers, and in Florida, where
he spends part of his winters, this fascina
tion exposes him regularly to a
bevy of
socialites. Buffeted back and forth between
theater officialdom and Social Registerdom,
Abbott has done well to retain his hickishness�which makes him, after all, a
legend
in the theater.
"People often ask me how I came to be
fond of the theater, if I have any relatives
who were in the business. And I say yes,"
as he once told a friend, "because I had a
great grandfather who was a Methodist
minister. His picture, hanging on the wall,
as I remembered it, with very firm mouth,
looked much the same as the daguerreo
types of the old-time Shakespearean actors;
and after all, it is the same business, the
same racket�selling something to an audi
ence."
To some members of his audience, Ab
bott is not selling as much as he is throw
ing something at them. But others, the
majority, find the Abbott Touch in tempo
with the times and, if the truth were
known, they are
actually waiting for him
to get his hands on Tallulah Bankhead and
Gertrude Lawrence. Then, Tallulah will
have to reach deep down and Gertie wfll
have to step higher and higher.

EXECUTIVE COUNCIL MEETING
Summary of What Transpired at a Recent Session
Meeting of March 8, 1948
The Executive Council met in New York
on March 8, 1948. Twelve members and one
former member of the Council were
present.
The Secretary read to the Council a com
munication
relating to the possible establish
ment of a
chapter of Psi Upsilon at Otterbein College; certain material pertaining to
the matter of the possible induction of gradu
ate students into the various chapters of the
Fraternity; and various matters of general
correspondence.
The Treasurer rendered an oral report.
The President reported that work would
be undertaken in the near future with refer
ence to the annual communication to the Con
vention. He also reported with regard to cer
tain miscellaneous correspondence, the fiftysecond consecutive annual "Little Chi" din
ner held in New York on
January 16, 1948,
and on functions held by the alumni of the
Theta and Delta Delta Chapters.
Brother Burleigh read the reports of his re
cent visits to the Rho Chapter and the Mu
Chapter. He also read reports which he had
prepared in regard to the situation of Psi
Upsilon in the Chicago area and with refer
ence to the probable petition of the Diamond

Charles Philip Spooner, Rho '94
The Diamond learned only recently that
Charles PhUip Spooner, Rho '94, died during
the summer of 1947, at Madison, Connecticut,
where he had made his home for some
years.
Brother Spooner received his A.B. from
Princeton University in 1892 and his LL.B.
from the University in
'
1894. Returning to
Princeton, he took his A.M. there in 1895.
His passing recalls another illustration of the
Charles P. Spooner, Rho '94
fascination the fratemity system holds for
alumni who had their undergraduate years at
Harvard, Yale and Princeton. At the latter,
the class traditionally is the center of interest,
while at colleges and universities generally the
fraternity brings aU classes together, as well
as the alumni, into a bond of wide common
interest. In past periods the interest of Alpha
and Beta men in their alumni years in the
activity of Psi Upsilon groups has been often
remarked. In the career of Charles P. Spooner
we have an
example of a Princeton alumnus,
eagerly embracing the opportunities of frater
nity life.
Fortunately, Spooner himself gave an in
teresting account of his fratemity activities in
The Diamond for the March and June issues
of 1938. The two articles related largely to
the part he played in the dramatic birth of
the Rho Chapter. It is possible to add now
that probably no incident in his career was
a
greater challenge to his character and abUity.
The Rho incident at the time far outran
Wisconsin and Psi Upsilon boundaries, for it
attracted over a
period of several years the

attention of the entire college world. It aroused
some of the most exciting debates ever heard
in our convention and chapter halls. In these
Spooner took a
leading part, including a
country-wide visit to the chapter roll.
The Rho incident did not revolve around
Wisconsin as a
university, nor of the qualifi
cation and desirability of the petitioning group,
nor of their change of allegiance. The debate .
was over the question of Western extension.
Spooner in his articles summarized the
points of tiie debate. The East contended that
its non-coeducational and private type of
older institutions was the region in which Psi
Upsilon ought to confine its activities; that
sooner or later mistakes would be made by
further western extension; and that Psi Upsilon
might become cumbersome and difficult to
manage.
As a Princeton alumnus with a Wisconsin
background Spooner found himself in a rather
difficult role. The conventions of 1893, 1894,
and 1895 submitted the petition to a vote of
the chapters, and approval by the chapters
came
finally in February 1896. The Iota, Phi
and the Mu then welcomed a
regional brother
chapter, to be followed later by the Epsilon
in 1902, the Theta Theta in 1916, the Zeta
Zeta in 1935, and the Epsilon Nu in 1943.
Spooner's Psi Upsilon activity after such a
dynamic start never faltered. As a
practicing
lawyer in Seattle he drafted the first petition
for the Theta Theta. When his father, John
C. Spooner, Rho '64, retired from the U.S.
Senate, he joined his father's law firm in
New York City. Elected to the Executive
Council in 1922 he served continuously until
1936, and as vice-president from 1923 to 1928.
A regular attendant at meetings, delegate to
the Annual Conventions, presiding over the
